        <title type="text">Has isotope labelling been used to trace material from carpospores to the gametophyte generation in red algae?</title>
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="marine-biology" />
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="algae" />
        <author>
            <name>Nhiệt</name>
            <uri>https://biology.stackexchange.com/users/132374</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://biology.stackexchange.com/questions/119775/has-isotope-labelling-been-used-to-trace-material-from-carpospores-to-the-gameto" />
        <published>2026-10-26T02:23:46Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-26T02:23:46Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>Has isotope labelling been used to trace material from carpospores to the gametophyte generation in red algae? In florideophyte red algae (e.g. Polysiphonia), carpospores grow into tetrasporophytes, which produce tetraspores that grow into gametophytes. Has any study traced an isotope label (e.g. ¹⁵N or ¹³C) across these phases to see how much of the original material remains in the gametophyte? I found work on nutrient transfer from gametophyte to carposporophyte, but nothing beyond that</p>

        </summary>

        <updated>2026-10-26T12:04:58Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>Besides encoding proteins, RNA can fold into complex structures to perform many different functions. Examples include tRNA, rRNA, and IRES (internal ribosome entry sites). These structures are formed via internal basepairing. I am curious if we just replace the base paired regions of an IRES with other pairs like replacing C-G with T-A or G-C, while maintaining the basic architecture of the stemloop, will it still work properly?

        <title type="text">Why do adjacent synonymous codons preserve information about the in-frame antisense amino acid?</title>
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="genetics" />
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="molecular-biology" />
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="dna" />
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="bioinformatics" />
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="translation" />
        <author>
            <name>Michael Goldstein</name>
            <uri>https://biology.stackexchange.com/users/132340</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://biology.stackexchange.com/questions/119771/why-do-adjacent-synonymous-codons-preserve-information-about-the-in-frame-antise" />
        <published>2026-10-23T15:52:33Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-23T15:52:33Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>When we look at codon usage bias (CUB) or do standard codon optimization (like Max-CAI), we almost always treat a gene as a single-stranded mRNA string. In the standard genetic code, 64 codons map to 21 outcomes (20 amino acids + stop), which leaves 64 - 21 = 43 degrees of synonymous freedom.</p>
<p>However, in genomic DNA, every sense codon is physically paired with its antiparallel reverse-complement triplet on the opposite strand. Because the antiparallel strand is read 5' to 3' in the opposite direction, the 3rd (wobble) base of the sense codon is the 1st (leading) base of the in-frame antisense triplet.</p>
<p>To put this in plain undergraduate biology terms, take the 6 synonymous codons for Leucine on the sense strand and look at what they code for on the reverse-complement strand (in the same reading frame):</p>
<pre><code>Sense (5'-&gt;3')          Antisense (5'-&gt;3')
CTT (Leu)       &lt;--&gt;    AAG (Lys)
CTC (Leu)       &lt;--&gt;    GAG (Glu)
TTA (Leu)       &lt;--&gt;    TAA (Stop)
CTA (Leu)       &lt;--&gt;    TAG (Stop)
TTG (Leu)       &lt;--&gt;    CAA (Gln)
CTG (Leu)       &lt;--&gt;    CAG (Gln)
</code></pre>
<p>On the sense strand, all six mean &quot;Leucine&quot;. On the opposite strand, they split into four completely different channels (Lys, Glu, Stop, Gln), leaving only two pairs (TTA/CTA and TTG/CTG) that are still synonymous on both strands. Across the entire genetic code table, if you specify the amino-acid channel on both strands at once, 48 out of the 64 codons have only one possible triplet (singletons), and only 8 binary pairs (16 codons) remain degenerate—shrinking the synonymous space from 43 dimensions down to 8.</p>
<p>I was testing an open-source Python audit from a recent preprint on this duplex codon structure (<a href="https://zenodo.org/records/23508081/files/codon_torus_real_audit_v3.py?download=1" rel="nofollow noreferrer">codon_torus_real_audit_v3.py</a>, Logvinovich &amp; Perez 2026, <a href="https://zenodo.org/records/23508081" rel="nofollow noreferrer">https://zenodo.org/records/23508081</a>) which evaluates consecutive codon transitions (how much the choice of codon at position i-1 predicts the choice of codon at position i) across 9.83 million held-out codon transitions in 9 RefSeq genomes (E. coli, B. subtilis, yeast, Arabidopsis, Drosophila, mouse, human T2T, etc.) without using synthetic Monte Carlo shuffles.</p>
<p>Two empirical results from the real RefSeq coding sequences stood out to me:</p>
<ol>
<li><p>Even after factoring out the protein's amino-acid sequence (dipeptide bias), consecutive codons are not independent: the synonymous choice of codon i-1 significantly predicts the identity of the next amino acid at position i (d2b &gt; 0 across all 9 species, p &lt; 10^-300).</p>
</li>
<li><p>When you measure the sequential &quot;synonymous&quot; correlation between adjacent codons (knowing the current amino acid at position i, how much does the previous codon i-1 predict which synonymous codon is used at position i?), 74.1% to 88.5% of that sequential synonymous information (82.5% in Human T2T and 83.2% in E. coli) is carried by the reverse-complement amino-acid channel on the antisense strand. Furthermore, when you recode genes using deterministic Max-CAI optimization (replacing every amino acid with its single most frequent codon, which wipes out this sequential context to zero), the transition log-likelihood under the wild-type reference kernel drops below zero in 77% to 98.7% of genes (96% in human).</p>
</li>
</ol>
<p>Now, part of that 74%–88% share is a direct algebraic consequence of the genetic code table: because 48 of 64 codons are uniquely fixed once you know both the sense and antisense amino-acid channels, any biological mechanism that creates codon-pair preference at the 3rd (wobble) position will automatically register in the antisense 1st-position reading frame.</p>
<p><strong>My question:</strong></p>
<p>Given that the vast majority of eukaryotic and prokaryotic genes do not code for functional proteins on their in-frame antisense strand, what known molecular mechanism—such as tRNA wobble-pair sterics in the ribosome A/P sites, DNA duplex repair/mutational asymmetry between transcribed and non-transcribed strands, or suppression of antisense cryptic translation (like those antisense TAA/TAG stops opposite TTA/CTA)—drives adjacent codon transitions to selectively partition across those specific reverse-complement channels, and why does single-codon Max-CAI optimization consistently violate this native transition grammar?</p>
<p><strong>Reference:</strong>
Logvinovich, V., &amp; Perez, J.-C. (2026). The Double-Stranded Codon Torus: Duplex Mirror Fibration of DNA Coding Space, Markovian Lumpability, and Information-Theoretic Consequences. Zenodo. <a href="https://zenodo.org/records/23508081" rel="nofollow noreferrer">https://zenodo.org/records/23508081</a></p>

        </summary>
    </entry>

XM_049506593.1  TTGATCTTCAAAAGCCACAAACTGAGCTTGATGGCAAGGCATGTGCTGCTGTGGGCCAGA

</code></pre>
<p>I need to design primers to amplify a partial mRNA of the ortholog of delta-1-pyrroline-5-carboxylate synthase (P5CS) in a hypothetical Solanaceae species &quot;X&quot; with no available sequence. I have a Clustal alignment (360 columns) of six Solanaceae P5CS partial mRNAs: NM_001326050.1, XM_060322531.1, XM_049506593.1, XM_055964307.1, JN606861.1, XM_049552827.1.</p>
<p><strong>Alignment analysis</strong></p>
<ul>
<li>Columns 1–60 are full of gaps and only ~12% of columns are identical, so I avoided them.</li>
<li>From column 61 onward there are no gaps and 63–77% of columns are identical in all six sequences.</li>
<li>I placed the primers in columns 227–346, where 93 of 120 columns (~78%) are identical in all six sequences. In this region, four sequences are 91.7–95.8% identical to NM_001326050.1; XM_049552827.1 is the most divergent (81.7%).</li>
<li>No fully conserved stretch of 20 nt exists in the alignment (the longest is 14 nt), so I used IUPAC degenerate bases.</li>
<li>I translated the sequences in three frames; only the frame starting at column 63 has no stop codon in all six sequences. All 8 degenerate positions are synonymous (7 at codon position 3, 1 at position 1).</li>
</ul>
<p><strong>My primers (5'→3')</strong></p>
<ul>
<li><strong>F1 (outer forward):</strong> TYTGGTSACYTCAGGTGCTG — columns 227–246, GC 50–60%, Tm 55.7–58.8 °C, 8 variants</li>
<li><strong>F2 (inner forward, optional):</strong> TCAGGTGCTGTWGGWGTTGG — columns 237–256, GC 55%, Tm 56.4–58.1 °C, 4 variants</li>
<li><strong>R (reverse):</strong> GCACAWGCYTTGCCATCRAG — columns 327–346, GC 50–60%, Tm 56.0–59.7 °C, 8 variants</li>
</ul>
<p>(R = A/G, W = A/T, Y = C/T, S = C/G. Primer R is the reverse complement of the coding strand at columns 327–346, target 5'-CTYGATGGCAARGCWTGTGC-3'.)</p>
<p>Tm was calculated with the nearest-neighbor model (SantaLucia 1998), 50 mM Na+, 0.5 µM primer, for every variant of each degenerate primer. I checked all six sequences against each primer and found zero mismatches.</p>
<p>Expected product: F1+R = 120 bp (columns 227–346); F2+R = 110 bp (columns 237–346). I proposed F2 for a semi-nested second round. Planned conditions: cDNA from DNase-treated total RNA, 0.5 µM each primer, 2 mM MgCl2, 35 cycles, annealing gradient 48–56 °C (start 52 °C).</p>
<p><strong>My instructor said this design is incorrect but did not say why.</strong> Some possibilities I wonder about:</p>
<ol>
<li>The amplicon (120 bp, of which ~40 bp are primer sequence) is too short to &quot;identify&quot; the partial mRNA of X. Should the primers be placed farther apart? For example, there is a region in columns 151–170 (GAMGAYTAGCACTTGGAAGA) that has only two degenerate positions and would give a ~196 bp product with R.</li>
<li>Is the number of degenerate positions (3, 2, and 3) too high, or should I have accepted a mismatch away from the 3' end instead of using degenerate bases?</li>
<li>Is the semi-nested design with F2 unnecessary or wrong for this problem?</li>
<li>Is something wrong with how I handled the reverse primer or the alignment column vs. nucleotide numbering (NM_001326050.1 has one gap in the first 60 columns, so nucleotide number = column − 1)?</li>
</ol>
<p>Could someone point out what is wrong with this design, or which criteria I should check when designing primers from an alignment for an unsequenced ortholog?</p>
<p>EDIT: Here is the alignment (6 Solanaceae P5CS mRNA sequences, 360 columns; &quot;*&quot; marks columns identical in all six sequences):</p>

        </summary>

        <title type="text">How are nucleoside analogue antivirals distributed within the body?</title>
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="biochemistry" />
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="pharmacokinetics" />
        <author>
            <name>哲煜黄</name>
            <uri>https://biology.stackexchange.com/users/67047</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://biology.stackexchange.com/questions/119766/how-are-nucleoside-analogue-antivirals-distributed-within-the-body" />
        <published>2026-10-20T13:07:26Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-20T13:07:26Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>Many drugs can freely cross the cell membranes. When taken, they are carried by the bloodstream and diffuse back and forth between the blood, interstitial fluids and the cytoplasm until they are evenly distributed in our body. But nucleoside analogues are different. While in native forms analogues like lamivudine can cross the cell membrane, once inside the cells they are phosphorylated into nucleotides (NMP, NDP, and NTP). Because phosphates are negatively charged, nucleotides can’t diffuse back to the bodily fluids. Does that mean nucleoside analogues are more easily sequestered in certain tissues compared to other drugs?
<a href="https://i.sstatic.net/Obj33q18.png" rel="nofollow noreferrer"><img src="https://i.sstatic.net/Obj33q18.png" alt="phosphorylation of nucleoside analogues" /></a></p>

        </summary>
    </entry>

        <title type="text">Biogenic molecules that can't biodegrade</title>
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="decomposition" />
        <author>
            <name>Kevin Kostlan</name>
            <uri>https://biology.stackexchange.com/users/4321</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://biology.stackexchange.com/questions/119761/biogenic-molecules-that-cant-biodegrade" />
        <published>2026-10-18T21:52:23Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-20T02:51:42Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>Plastics are notorious for sticking around in the environment. But how close can we get to  natural biological &quot;forever chemicals&quot;?</p>
<p>Petrified wood and most fossils don't count. They are inorganic minerals deposited as the remains decay. But amber is an exception, an organic resin that lasts for 100+ million years.</p>
<p>Is amber very hard to biodegrade in, say, an industrial compost pile? Are there other examples of resistant biopolymers that almost nothing biological can degrade? <strong>Edit:</strong> I most interested in organic molecules, not bio minerals.</p>

        </summary>
    </entry>

        <title type="text">What physical or translational constraints limit conditional codon-bigram bias to exactly a ~30-codon window?</title>
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="genetics" />
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="molecular-biology" />
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="bioinformatics" />
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="translation" />
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="ribosome" />
        <author>
            <name>Billy Bolly</name>
            <uri>https://biology.stackexchange.com/users/131147</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://biology.stackexchange.com/questions/119749/what-physical-or-translational-constraints-limit-conditional-codon-bigram-bias-t" />
        <published>2026-10-12T07:45:25Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-16T08:35:49Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>In bioinformatics, models of codon usage bias (CUB) usually treat codon populations as static macroscopic properties determined by GC-content, mutational bias, or global translational efficiency. However, I recently came across a preprint and an open-source pipeline (Logvinovich &amp; Perez, 2026) that analyzed the sequential, conditional order of codons inside single-stranded open reading frames.</p>
<p>The authors ran an empirical codon-bigram transition model <span class="math-container">$P(c_{i+1}\vert{}c_i)$</span> on real, unmanipulated coding sequences directly from the NCBI RefSeq database across 13 diverse taxa (mammals, plants, fungi, bacteria, archaea). Since the pipeline is completely open-source, the math is reproducible. To ensure the results were not artifacts of synthetic simulations, they tested these real open reading frames against a strict ladder of Markovian and permutation null models (controlling for static codon usage, amino-acid order, folded nucleotide trigrams, and even preserving the exact populations of reverse-complement mirror pairs).</p>
<p>The statistical matrices show that a non-random conditional codon syntax exists across all 13 species, but it has a very strict physical boundary: the information-theoretic signal peaks at a medium-range scale of about 30 codons (~90 base pairs) and completely collapses to zero at a scale of 100 codons.</p>
<p>Since this is a pure mathematical observation on real-world genomic data (not simulated sequences) that survives strict local-block and compositional shuffles, it strongly implies a physical or biochemical constraint.</p>
<p><strong>My question:</strong></p>
<p>What known structural or evolutionary constraints in molecular biology perfectly match a ~30-codon (~90 bp) operational window? Does this scale specifically correlate with the physical length of the ribosomal mRNA transit tunnel, tRNA accommodation kinetics, or co-translational folding steps?</p>
<p><strong>References:</strong>
Logvinovich, V., &amp; Perez, J. C. (2026). From Form to Program: Medium-Range Conditional Codon Syntax Inside Real Genes. (Preprint &amp; Open-source Pipeline v13). Doi: <a href="https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23294002" rel="noreferrer">https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23294002</a></p>

        </summary>
    </entry>

        <title type="text">How can enzyme candidates be ranked by the population of catalytically competent conformers rather than a single structure?</title>
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="biochemistry" />
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="bioinformatics" />
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="enzymes" />
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="structural-biology" />
        <author>
            <name>steve</name>
            <uri>https://biology.stackexchange.com/users/131120</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://biology.stackexchange.com/questions/119747/how-can-enzyme-candidates-be-ranked-by-the-population-of-catalytically-competent" />
        <published>2026-10-09T22:25:15Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-09T22:25:15Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>Recent cryo-EM work on bacterial RNase P (<em>Nature</em>, Oct 2026, DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-11140-z) resolved 76 coexisting conformers of the RNA at ~3 Å and showed regulation works by shifting population weights — the active closed conformer rises from ~13% (apo) to ~43% (holo) on protein binding — rather than by rebuilding the structure. The catalytic function lives in the ensemble statistics.</p>
<p>This raises a practical question for candidate screening (ribozymes, and by extension enzymes): most screening and docking pipelines still score single structures — lowest-energy conformer, best docked pose. If function is a population property, single-structure scoring seems systematically wrong: a candidate with a slightly worse ground state but a large catalytically competent sub-population could outperform one with a better ground state and a narrow ensemble.</p>
<p>What I'm looking for:</p>
<ol>
<li>Are there established experimental or computational frameworks that rank candidates by ensemble properties — e.g., Boltzmann-weighted populations of competent states, or transient-intermediate accessibility — rather than single-structure scores?</li>
<li>What are the standard references? I know of Markov state models and ensemble docking, but I'm asking specifically about <em>ranking candidates against each other</em> by ensemble-derived quantities, and whether there's evidence this outperforms single-structure scoring in practice.</li>
</ol>
<p>Concrete anchor: the RNase P case above, where a heterogeneity-focused analysis captured even a transient intermediate (tertiary contact formed, catalytic domain unformed) — the kind of state a single-structure screen would never see.</p>

        </summary>
    </entry>

        <title type="text">Is drug resistance of herpes simplex much less likely than other viruses?</title>
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="virology" />
        <author>
            <name>哲煜黄</name>
            <uri>https://biology.stackexchange.com/users/67047</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://biology.stackexchange.com/questions/119734/is-drug-resistance-of-herpes-simplex-much-less-likely-than-other-viruses" />
        <published>2026-09-28T17:26:41Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-12T11:20:35Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>On the one hand, HSV is much larger and mutates more slowly than RNA viruses like HIV or influenza. On the other hand HSV has a very unusual life cycle. After infection, the virus quickly finds neuronal ganglia and hides there. Because there are only a limited number of ganglia and each cell harbors only a few copies, the genetic pool of the HSV viral reservoir is exceptionally small. During activation, HSV makes many copies by infecting skin cells, but infection of the skin is a one-way ticket for the virus: mutations picked up by viral offspring in skin cells won’t be passed on to the viral reservoirs. In other words, each reactivation is caused by new, treatment-naïve viruses. HSV also employs an unusual rolling circle strategy to replicate its DNA, which means the original copy is maintained in the viral reservoir.</p>
<p>So does this mean that if someone is infected with a drug-sensitive strain, he will never develop resistance no matter how many times he is treated?</p>

        </summary>
    </entry>

        <id>https://biology.stackexchange.com/q/100652</id>
        <re:rank scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com">17</re:rank>
        <title type="text">What kills a plant that requires winter dormancy if it is kept indoors all year?</title>
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="molecular-biology" />
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="cell-biology" />
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="botany" />
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="metabolism" />
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="plant-physiology" />
        <author>
            <name>cape1232</name>
            <uri>https://biology.stackexchange.com/users/65356</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://biology.stackexchange.com/questions/100652/what-kills-a-plant-that-requires-winter-dormancy-if-it-is-kept-indoors-all-year" />
        <published>2021-05-09T18:17:06Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-18T19:42:49Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>In bonsai practice, beginners will commonly purchase a juniper (often Juniperus procumbens 'Nana'), which is an outdoor tree, and keep it inside all year.  The tree invariably dies.  It is commonly explained to the beginners that this is because junipers are outdoor trees and require a winter dormancy.</p>
<p>My question is what exactly goes wrong that leads to the death of the plant?  Let's assume that the person gives the tree appropriate care, e.g. assume that desiccation or root rot or other more direct causes of death are not the reason.  (Of course, a valid answer is that it is impossible to give &quot;appropriate care&quot; for some specific reason.)</p>
<p>I have two strong hypotheses in more detail but not in a rigorously scientifically biological detail.</p>
<ol>
<li><p>The first is that the warmth and low humidity of the indoor environment cause the plant to continue to transpire water and attempt to grow or maintain foliar mass while the reduced daylight hours signal the plant to &quot;do something&quot; (what, though?) that results in lower metabolic action.  And so the tree expends its stored energy (starches and sugars?).  Then, in spring, the when the tree tries to put on a strong flush of growth, it has nothing left to build on.  So it struggles and eventually dies.</p>
</li>
<li><p>The second is that there is a daily metabolic cycle that is disrupted when the tree is kept in the more or less constant indoor environment.  That is, there is a cycle that depends on the daily differences in temperature and humidity the tree experiences during daytime and nighttime.  Through my own measurements, I have found, for example, that the vapor pressure deficit (VPD) reduces to near zero outdoors during the night in springtime as temperatures drop and relative humidity rises.  This, I think, means the respiration demands on the tree are near zero.  That is not the case indoors where the VPD is more or less constant.</p>
</li>
</ol>
<p>Is either of those at all consistent with what really happens?  And what does really happen from a biological perspective? What part of the plant's metabolism fails?  Is there something that happens during dormancy that doesn't happen when it doesn't get a cold dormant period?  Is there something detrimental that happens when it should be dormant but isn't?</p>
<p>If anyone has any pointers to resources where I could do further research on this question, that would be much appreciated, too, and I will update here with any further information I can find.</p>

        </summary>
    </entry>

            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="molecular-genetics" />
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="virology" />
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="infectious-diseases" />
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="liver" />
        <author>
            <name>Amarylis Vaselaar</name>
            <uri>https://biology.stackexchange.com/users/61825</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://biology.stackexchange.com/questions/96241/reason-for-partially-double-stranded-dna-of-hepatitis-b-virus" />
        <published>2020-10-09T16:46:11Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-20T08:32:47Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>According to my school biology textbook and also <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hepatitis_B_virus" rel="nofollow noreferrer">Wikipedia,</a> hepatitis B is the only Hepatitis virus to possess <em>partially double-stranded</em> DNA.
I found an image from <a href="https://microbiologyinfo.com/hepatitis-b-virus-structure-epidemiology-symptoms-pathogenesis-diagnosis-treatment-and-vaccines/" rel="nofollow noreferrer">here</a> <a href="https://i.sstatic.net/jrCqa.png" rel="nofollow noreferrer"><img src="https://i.sstatic.net/jrCqa.png" alt="partially double-stranded" /></a></p>
<p>What is the reason for the partially double-stranded DNA?</p>
<p>(It seems that it can be triple-stranded as well.)</p>
<p>I found this information in this research about <a href="https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC140969/" rel="nofollow noreferrer">duck hepatitis B virus</a></p>
<blockquote>
<p>Similar to classical retroviruses, viral assembly begins with the formation of intracellular nucleocapsid particles that specifically package the pgRNA. However, all hepadnaviruses undergo a maturation phase during their morphogenesis that is characterized by the reverse transcription of the pgRNA prior to membrane envelopment and secretion as extracellular virions, rather than subsequent to entry into new target cells, as is the case for classical retroviruses (for a review, see reference 20). Thus, secreted hepadnaviral virions contain only the “mature” ds DNA, whereas intracellular pools of nucleocapsids contain nucleic acid species from all the intermediate stages of reverse transcription ranging from only pgRNA to single (minus)-stranded (ss) DNA as well as ds DNA, a fundamental observation made by Summers and Mason 2 decades ago (22)</p>
</blockquote>
<ul>
<li><p>What is the special advantage of having such a genome?</p>
</li>
<li><p>are there any other organisms with partially double stranded DNA or partially double stranded RNA as well?</p>
</li>
</ul>

        </summary>
    </entry>

        <title type="text">Oxygen dissociation curve and temperature</title>
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="respiration" />
            <category scheme="https://biology.stackexchange.com/tags" term="breathing" />
        <author>
            <name>deechitpoudel</name>
            <uri>https://biology.stackexchange.com/users/30691</uri>
        </author>
        <link rel="alternate" href="https://biology.stackexchange.com/questions/57287/oxygen-dissociation-curve-and-temperature" />
        <published>2017-03-14T16:59:32Z</published>
        <updated>2026-10-24T09:56:15Z</updated>
        <summary type="html">
            <p>Say, we have a container with a mixture of gases at temperature <span class="math-container">$T$</span>. The concentration of oxygen is <span class="math-container">$C_{O_2}$</span> and its partial pressure is <span class="math-container">$P_{O_2}$</span>. We then introduce a sample of deoxygenated hemoglobin in that container. A certain percentage <span class="math-container">$S_{O_2}$</span> of the sample gets saturated  with oxygen at equilibrium. Afterwards, we increase the temperature of the gas in the container keeping everything else constant. What will happen to the <span class="math-container">$S_{O_2}$</span>?</p>
<p>I know that the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve (ODC) shifts rightward with an increase in temperature and this right shift signifies the increasing denaturation of <span class="math-container">$\text{Hb}-\text{O}_{2}$</span> bond at higher temperature. What I ask here is, since <span class="math-container">$P_{O_2}$</span> also increases with temperature, what effect would dominate - the drop in <span class="math-container">$S_{O_2}$</span> in y-axis due to the rightward shift of the curve or its rise due to the increment in <span class="math-container">$P_{O_2}$</span> in x-axis?</p>
<p>Wouldn't it have been better to use a <span class="math-container">$C_{O_2}$</span> vs <span class="math-container">$S_{O_2}$</span> curve instead to describe the physiology? Because in our example of increasing temperature, we not only have to switch ODC graphs, each specific to a certain temperature, but also have to switch the x-axis value (as <span class="math-container">$P_{O_2}$</span> also rises with <span class="math-container">$T$</span>) to find the new <span class="math-container">$S_{O_2}$</span> value. Likewise, since <span class="math-container">$P_{O_2}$</span> is a function of <span class="math-container">$C_{O_2}$</span> and <span class="math-container">$T$</span>, shouldn't temperature dependent <span class="math-container">$C_{O_2}$</span> vs <span class="math-container">$S_{O_2}$</span> curves more fundamentally describe the physiology?</p>

        </summary>
    </entry>
